Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Infra), Lena Brooks (Support), Maya Singh (Orion ML Platform), Ethan Cole (Orion Staff ML), Priya Kapoor (Orion Sec), Jon Torres (Orion SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
- Deep dive on KV cache eviction patterns and paging under multi-prefix workloads.
- Orion sees high token latency during long-context sessions; suspected cache thrash and prefix collisions.
- Discussed mitigations: segmenting cache by tenant, prefix hashing, prefetch windows, NVMe-backed spill, LRU vs LFU knobs, and quantization tradeoffs.
- Agreed on next steps: run a reproducible benchmark, share docs, schedule on-prem runtime check.

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery (Redwood AE): okay, hello everyone, thanks for carving time. we'll do a focused runtime deep dive on the kv layer today, specifically the paging / eviction patterns you've been seeing, maya if you want to quickly frame the problem from orion side?
[00:18] Maya (Orion): yeah thanks avery. so basically, we're seeing intermittent latency spikes when we hit long context flows, like 8k-20k token threads, but not consistently. it's kinda correlated with concurrent users who have a lot of reused prefixes, basically similar prompts with different user ids, so--we suspect your kv cache is being evicted then paging and then the runtime stalls.
[00:42] Diego (Redwood SE): right, good. do you have any telemetry yet? traces, eviction counts, or nvme io stats? even a flame graph?
[00:50] Ethan (Orion): we pulled some traces, yes. we have a CSV of per-request token latency, and some vmstat iostat dumps. we can share. the pattern looks like: stable 60-80ms/token then a 500-1200ms spike for a small batch of requests, then back to normal. seems aligned with cache miss storms.
[01:12] Diego: okay that's classic cache thrash. quick sanity check on config — are you using dedicated pools or hosted? and are you running private on-prem or vpc?
[01:22] Maya: private deployment in our vpc, running on 8xA100 nodes with local nvme. we opted for q4 quantization for cost reasons.
[01:31] Samir (Redwood): a couple things to flag there — quantization can increase decoding latency slightly if kernels are suboptimal for q4, but the big factor for thrash is prefix reuse + small kv capacity per GPU. when many similar prefixes map to same cache slots you get eviction storms.
[01:50] Priya (Orion Sec): quick sec question — any of these mitigations require sending more data to redwood control plane? we need to keep data residency compliance.
[02:00] Avery: no, everything we propose for on-prem runs in your VPC. we may share anonymized telemetry CSVs out of band, but the runtime changes are local.
[02:10] Jon (Orion SRE): cool. we want to avoid disk thrash; our NVMe is on node-local, we prefer mmap-based spill to avoid synchronous fsyncs but open to recommendations.
[02:22] Diego: okay great. let me walk through the kv architecture at a high level — i'll be brief then jump to mitigation strategies. the runtime keeps a per-gpu kv store in host memory sharded by key hashed into a fixed-size ring-backed slab allocator. by default we use LRU-ish eviction with a generation counter; we also have LFU experimental mode. when the working set exceeds in-memory capacity we page to an nvme local spill file or, in hosted mode, to a networked cache.
[02:52] Diego: the important bit is prefix reuse: the system indexes using the full prefix token sequence hash, which is great for accuracy but sensitive to small variations — similar prefixes with different user ids become distinct keys. if your workload has thousands of slightly different prefixes, the effective working set balloons and you hit eviction.
[03:12] Ethan: is there a way to canonicalize prefixes? we often attach a user-id at the front.
[03:18] Diego: yeah, prefix normalization is a common approach — strip or token-map ephemeral ids before hashing. but that requires application-level changes or a middleware layer. another approach is to use a two-level cache: a prefix-normalized microcache for recent prefixes and a canonical full-kv store.
[03:34] Maya: hmm we can't change all clients quickly. we need runtime-level mitigations first.
[03:40] Diego: understood. runtime options we discussed: 1) increase in-memory kv capacity (larger slab, tune batch size), 2) enable prefetch window — when a prefix is used, prefetch adjacent likely keys (n-gram lookahead), 3) use probabilistic eviction (LFU with decay) to keep frequently reused prefixes, 4) segment the kv store by hashed tenant/prefix namespace to reduce cross-tenant eviction, 5) improve spill/paging layer by using async NVMe io and a write-back buffer to avoid blocking serving threads.
[04:12] Samir: i'll add — for on-prem with local NVMe, mmap plus O_DIRECT can reduce kernel buffer copies but you need to tune fio pattern and ensure your filesystem isn't doing aggressive background GC (btrfs/compressed layers can be bad). ext4/xfs on a raw nvme partition is usually best.
[04:33] Maya: any experiments around hybrid storage where hot prefixes kept in ram and cold prefixes on nvme with fast prefetch?
[04:39] Diego: yes, that's the default pattern for spill. we maintain a hot set and a cold set. the problem in your case is the hot set keeps getting polluted by near-unique prefixes. Prefetch helps if you can predict sequence continuation; we use Markov-ish n-gram scoring on previous runs to prioritize prefetch candidates. it's not perfect and has a CPU cost.
[04:58] Ethan: how expensive is the prefetch CPU-wise? we have limited CPU headroom on the inference nodes; we allocate most cycles to kernel dispatch.
[05:06] Diego: depends on window size. a small window (2-4 next keys) is cheap — a few percent CPU. large windows with scoring across thousands of candidates will add tens of percent. we recommend starting small and measuring.
[05:20] Priya: security — does prefetch risk leaking prefix data across tenants?
[05:25] Avery: good callout. prefetch and segmenting by tenant namespace are combined — we never prefetch across tenant boundaries. prefetch only considers local-tenant priors, unless you explicitly enable cross-tenant sharing (not recommended for regulated data).
[05:37] Maya: you mentioned LFU with decay — we tried LRU and it seemed to evict something that later was needed again, causing the spikes. would LFU be better?
[05:47] Diego: LFU can retain frequently reused prefixes even if not recently used, which helps for workloads with periodic reuse. The tilt is that LFU requires tracking counters which increases memory and CPU overhead. Decay is important to avoid forever-growth of counters. In practice we see LFU reduce thrash for prefix-reuse workloads, but it's workload-dependent. we can flip it in your runtime and run A/B.
[06:10] Jon: will changing eviction policy require a restart or redeploy?
[06:13] Diego: policy flips are hot by design — we allow runtime toggles with safe migration. there may be a transient as stats warm up, but no full restart.
[06:21] Maya: paging — when the kv spills to nvme we saw a huge latency bump, is that because of synchronous reads?
[06:28] Diego: yep, by default the spill layer did some blocking reads for correctness. we have an async fallback mode where reads schedule io and return a partial-generated response (or stall at decoding boundary) while io completes. for your SLA needs, we usually push async read + speculative decode where the runtime predicts continuation and streams partial tokens until the exact kv arrives, then corrects if mismatch — tradeoff is occasional minor hallucination or token correction.
[06:55] Ethan: speculative decode sounds risky for correctness-sensitive bios responses. we can't do that for all flows. can we tag namespaces as strict (no speculative) and best-effort?
[07:04] Diego: absolutely, we support per-route SLO classes — strict routes block until kv is loaded, best-effort allow speculation, and a middle ground uses low-latency prefetching to reduce blocking.
[07:15] Maya: about the NVMe behavior: we prefer mmap with O_DIRECT to avoid page cache duplicates. are you seeing copying between kernel page cache and user space?
[07:25] Samir: in earlier builds we did see double copies; current runtime uses mmap and direct io paths for spill files but a misconfiguration in the local distro can force fallback to buffered ios. We'll share a checklist.
[07:37] Lena (Support): i'll paste the nvme checklist link in the follow-up — it includes fio patterns, mount flags, and kernel tunables.
[07:44] Ethan: quantization — we are on q4 to save memory, could quantization be making kv entries larger or different shape which affects eviction?
[07:53] Diego: quantization mainly affects inference kernel memory for activations and KV representation when we compress keys/values. With q4 we store compressed kv values which reduces per-key size, which should help. but some q4 kernels have slightly different token generation timing which can amplify perceived latency spikes when mixed with paging. Rarely quantization increases per-kv metadata size due to alignment/padding, but in general q4 helps memory footprint.
[08:18] Maya: how about prefix hashing collisions? are we losing keys because of hash table overflows?
[08:24] Diego: we use a high-quality 64-bit hash but with a fixed table load factor. If your working set hits high occupancy we can table-resize or use chained buckets. collisions are rare but when they happen they can cause silent miss patterns. we can enable aggressive resizing for your deployment. there's a memory/time tradeoff.
[08:43] Priya: from security perspective, any change to hashing or canonicalization could change observable behavior; will you document determinism so we can audit?
[08:50] Avery: yes, we'll provide a diffed architecture doc and determinism notes. all runtime changes are auditable in the release notes.
[08:58] Ethan: curious — you mentioned tenant-segmentation. will that split capacity per tenant and risk underutilization?
[09:06] Diego: it can. segmentation prevents cross-tenant eviction but lowers statistical multiplexing benefits. we often implement soft-segmentation: reserve minimum per-tenant and allow burstable shared pool. that gives guarantees while still using spare capacity.
[09:20] Maya: ok that sounds promising. is there a quick config we can try without deep infra changes?
[09:26] Diego: yes — we can flip policy to LFU+decay, increase in-memory slab by 20%, and enable async spill with a 50ms read timeout before partial fallback. That combo often reduces the observed spikes. it doesn't require redeploys, only a rolling config push.
[09:42] Jon: for baseline reproducible test, what should we run? we plan to generate synthetic traffic with our real prefixes.
[09:49] Diego: ideal benchmark: 48k request trace over 30 minutes with the real prefix distribution, capture per-token latency, eviction count, spill reads, and nvme iops. include cold-start sequence and steady-state. We'll provide a benchmark harness script.
[10:07] Maya: can you also instrument prefix similarity heatmap? like how many unique prefixes per minute and overlap?
[10:13] Diego: yes we'll add that. we already have a small tool that groups prefixes by cosine embedding of tokenized prefix; it's noisy but helpful.
[10:22] Ethan: aside — is there any benefit to changing the hash granularity from full-token sequence to say last N tokens? some of our prefixes share endings rather than starts.
[10:31] Diego: yes, suffix-based hashing can catch cases where the tail contains the shared context. our system supports configurable hashing window (full, prefix-lastN, suffix-lastN, rolling). it's a tradeoff: smaller window increases collisions but increases effective reuse. We can try last 32 tokens as an experiment.
[10:50] Priya: i want to circle back to compliance — none of these experiments should leak or persist PHI outside Orion. confirm the spill files stay on node-local encrypted nvme and keys are local to customer KMS?
[11:00] Avery: confirmed — on-prem deployments keep spill files local. we support dm-crypt and integrate with customer KMS for key provisioning. we never ship raw spill files to Redwood control plane unless explicitly allowed.
[11:12] Maya: excellent. what about monitoring — what dashboards should we look at? we want a small set of SLOs to detect thrash early.
[11:20] Diego: three things: 95/99 token latency, eviction rate (evictions/sec), and spill-read latency (p50/p95). add NVMe iops and queue depth. set alert when eviction/sec > threshold or p95 token latency > SLA.
[11:34] Samir: also track unique-prefix rate and top-k prefixes by freq; a rising unique-prefix/sec is a leading indicator of working set growth.
[11:42] Maya: great. can you give a rough timeline for the config push and the repro benchmark?
[11:47] Avery: we can run the benchmark and deliver initial results in ~7 business days after we get your prefix CSV and access to a test node. config push can be staged next day but we prefer benchmark first.
[11:57] Ethan: okay we'll share artifacts by Monday. Jon will coordinate infra.
[12:02] Diego: quick note on future work — we're prototyping a compaction pass that coalesces near-duplicate prefixes using fuzzy token merges; early results show 20-40% reduced working set for templated prompts. not GA yet but we can try as an experiment.
[12:18] Maya: that could be huge for us. do you need more logs to build the merge heuristics?
[12:24] Diego: samples of 10k prefixes and their tokenized forms help a lot. we'll keep everything on-prem if you prefer.
[12:30] Avery: all right let's wrap up. i'll summarize next steps in the follow-up with links.
[12:36] Maya: thanks everyone appreciate it.
[12:38] Avery: thanks, talk soon.
